definition: The heroic people of the North Caucasus sagas, a quarrelsome warband of brothers and champions. The name is Iranian in origin, and each community tells the Nart stories in its own language and version.
An Iranian-speaking people of the central North Caucasus, descended from the Alans. Their Nart epic, the Narty kaddzhytæ, is the best-known and most studied version, though it is not the only one.
A group of Northwest Caucasian peoples, including Kabardians, Adyghe and Shapsugs, whose Nart epic is among the richest. Circassian tales often preserve details that Ossetian versions smooth out.
The Narts' truth-testing cup in Ossetian tradition, kept by the wise Alagata clan. It rises to the lips of a hero who speaks honestly and refuses a liar, making it a symbol of honour.
The mother and matriarch of the Narts, known as Satana in Ossetian. She is wise, beautiful and sometimes ruthless, and her counsel holds the warband's household together across many episodes.
The stone-born trickster hero of the Narts, called Soslan in Ossetian. Small, dark and cunning, he steals fire, outwits giants and survives by wit rather than strength.
The steel-bodied storm hero of the Ossetian Narts, son of Khamyts. Tempered by the smith Kurdalagon, he is nearly invulnerable, quarrels with the Narts and dies in several told ways.
The Ossetian trickster of the Nart cycle, son of Dzerassae. He stirs quarrels, betrays secrets and is blamed for Soslan's death; his grief is linked to the making of the fandyr.
The Circassian smith god of the Narts, whose Ossetian counterpart is Kurdalagon. He tempers heroes, forges their weapons and quarrels with Setenaya in one remembered tale.
The mountain range and region between the Black and Caspian Seas, home to the Ossetians, Circassians, Abkhaz, Balkars, Karachays and many other peoples who keep the Nart sagas.
